title: Heat treatment of steel: annealing, quenching and tempering
examples: What is the difference between annealing and quenching?

explain.say: A Japanese swordsmith heats a blade until it glows, then plunges it into water with a hiss. A blacksmith lets a horseshoe cool slowly by the fire. Same steel, very different results. The difference is the cooling rate. Look at the three cooling curves, all starting from 850 degrees.

draw.text: Heat treatment of steel: annealing, quenching and tempering
All start at 850 °C, where steel is austenite (FCC)

explain.say: At 850 degrees, plain carbon steel is austenite, the FCC form, which holds carbon in solution. Annealing means cooling very slowly in the furnace, the gentle curve. The carbon has time to move and forms soft ferrite and pearlite. The steel ends up soft and easy to machine. After ten minutes it is still above 700 degrees. See it?

Quenching in water is the cliff on the left: down to near room temperature in well under a minute. The carbon is trapped, and the iron is forced into a strained structure called martensite. It is very hard but brittle, like glass. Air cooling, called normalising, sits in between. Would you want a spring made of brittle martensite?

draw.text: Quench: below 100 °C within seconds; martensite forms

explain.say: No, it could shatter! So we temper it: reheat to a moderate temperature, say 200 to 650 degrees, and hold. Some carbon escapes the strain, the brittleness falls, and toughness returns, at the cost of a little hardness. Follow the chain on the board.

draw.text: Higher tempering temperature: softer but tougher

explain.say: Brilliant work. Quench and temper is how springs, axles, chisels and gear teeth are made. Exam tip: only steel with enough carbon, roughly above 0.3 percent, hardens well by quenching. Challenge: why might a thick part crack when quenched in water but not in oil?

draw.text: Oil quenches more gently: fewer cracks and less distortion

faq.a: Heating steel into the austenite range and cooling it very slowly, usually in the furnace. It makes the steel soft, ductile and easy to machine and removes internal stresses.
Heating steel above its critical temperature and letting it cool in still air. It gives a finer, more even grain than annealing and slightly higher strength.
A very hard, brittle structure formed when steel is quenched from austenite so fast that carbon cannot escape. The trapped carbon distorts the iron lattice.
asks: what is the difference between annealing and quenching

faq.a: Quenched martensite is too brittle for use. Tempering reheats it to a moderate temperature, which relieves strain and restores toughness while keeping much of the hardness.

faq.q: Why can quenching crack a part?
faq.a: The surface cools and transforms before the core, creating big internal stresses. Thick sections and sharp corners in a fast water quench are most at risk, so oil or polymer quenchants are gentler.

facts: Martensite forms only when steel is cooled faster than its critical cooling rate.

quiz.say: You need a steel part to be as soft as possible for machining. Which treatment?
quiz.show: Which treatment makes steel softest for machining?
quiz.why: Slow furnace cooling forms soft ferrite and coarse pearlite.

wrong.1: Quenching makes hard martensite, the opposite of what you want.
wrong.2: A low-temperature temper keeps the part very hard.

quiz.say: What does tempering do to quenched steel?

options.show: Raises toughness and lowers hardness a little
options.say: Raises toughness and lowers hardness a little

options.show: Makes it harder and more brittle
options.say: Makes it harder and more brittle

quiz.why: Tempering relieves the strained martensite, trading some hardness for much better toughness.

wrong.1: That is what quenching does, not tempering.
wrong.2: Tempering stays below the temperature where austenite forms.
